Omar Lizardo[1]

University of California, Los Angeles

Clayton Childress

University of British Columbia

 

Abstract

In this paper, we extend the Network Variety Model (NVM), the main
framework linking diverse social networks to broader cultural
participation, by addressing two gaps: a narrow focus on public arts and
insufficient attention to network composition, particularly political
ideology. Considering both conventional public arts participation and
everyday, solitary leisure (like reading or gardening), we find that
network variety operates differently across domains: strong-tie variety
is the primary driver of public arts participation, whereas for solitary
leisure activities, weak-tie variety is the primary driver, and
strong-tie variety is a deterrent. Most significantly, our study shows
that the association between political ideology (liberal or
conservative) and cultural engagement is fully explained by the
ideological makeup of personal networks, as measured by connections to
ideologically aligned positions, suggesting that cultural stratification
is organized relationally—through patterned, ideologically sorted social
environments—rather than solely via personal political beliefs and
related psychological dispositions. We close by outlining the
implications of the results and suggesting avenues for future research.

Keywords: Network Variety; Network Composition; Ideological Sorting;
Cultural Participation; Solitary Leisure

 

Introduction

How do personal networks shape taste and cultural participation? On this
question, the Erickson’s (1996) network variety mode (NVM) has been the
main guiding framework. According to the NVM, ties that span multiple
positions in the social structure provide greater familiarity with
different cultural forms, thereby expanding participation and taste
through broader exposure; in short “network variety leads to cultural
variety.” Overall, a large body of research consistently supports this
core proposition across national contexts, cultural domains, and
methodological approaches. The NVM has also generated useful extensions,
explaining, for example, how networks serve as a resource in the
diffusion of cultural forms (Mark 1998), how network variety converts
into cultural capital (Garrett 2016; Relish 1997), and how the outcome
of weak ties is also a cultural strength of popular or “weak” culture
(Lizardo 2006; Schultz and Breiger 2010).

Despite broad consensus on the NVM's predictive utility and wide
applicability, its core insights can be expanded in two generative ways.
First, many studies of culture and networks operationalize cultural
participation narrowly, relying on attendance-based measures tied to
conventional arts and cultural industries. While analytically tractable,
this approach risks classifying a substantial share of the population as
culturally “inactive,” overlooking everyday and solitary forms of
leisure (e.g., reading at home) that are less directly connected to
aesthetic institutions yet still constitute meaningful patterns of
cultural engagement. Second, work in the NVM tradition has focused
primarily on network variety—volume, range, and heterogeneity of
ties—while paying less attention to network composition, that is, the
extent to which personal networks are structured around particular
sociodemographic or ideological groups. In essence focusing on
quantitative variety rather than the qualitative heterogeneity of
personal networks. When qualitative variety has been incorporated, this
is usually reserved for a single dimension of association (typically
occupation) rather than looking across all relevant dimensions of
association (Blau 1977). This emphasis may obscure how qualitatively
different social environments shape cultural participation in distinct
ways.

In this paper, we address both of these issues. Substantively, we expand
the scope of cultural participation in networks to include not only
public arts activities but also more everyday, solitary leisure
practices. Methodologically, we introduce a group-based adaptation of
the position generator that captures both weak and strong ties across a
broad range of sociodemographic and ideological positions, including
race, gender, religiosity, urbanicity, and political orientation. This
approach preserves the analytic strengths of the usual occupation-based
position generator (Lin, Fu, and Hsung 2001) while defining social
position more broadly, allowing us to distinguish between network
variety and network composition as separate dimensions of personal
networks.

Using data from a quota sample of U.S. adults, we examine how weak- and
strong-tie network variety and composition relate to two distinct
domains of cultural engagement: public arts participation and everyday
solitary leisure. We find that network variety remains a robust
predictor of conventional arts participation, particularly for strong
ties, but operates differently across domains. For everyday solitary
leisure, weak- and strong-tie variety exert opposing effects,
challenging the assumption that network diversity uniformly increases
cultural participation. We also show that, second to variety, network
composition is structured by political ideology and plays an independent
role in shaping cultural engagement. Across both domains, the
association between respondents’ political ideology and participation is
fully mediated by the ideological composition of their personal
networks, indicating that cultural stratification operates via patterned
social environments rather than solely through individual dispositions.
Taken together, these findings extend the NVM by showing that both what
counts as cultural participation and how networks are measured shape
conclusions about the relationship between social structure and cultural
life.

Previous Work on the Link Between Networks and Cultural Consumption

The central hypothesis driving work on the effects of network ties on
cultural tastes and consumption patterns is Erickson’s (1996) Network
Variety Model (NVM). According to Erickson, the more diverse an
individual’s network connections are, the more varied their tastes and
cultural consumption habits will be. That is, network variety leads to
cultural variety (the variety principle). The primary mechanism behind
Erickson’s NVM is exposure: individuals whose networks span a wide range
of positions in the social structure are exposed to a broader range of
tastes and cultural pursuits associated with those positions, thereby
acquiring a working familiarity with those cultural styles. In her now
classic original study Erickson used data from a sample of respondents
in the Toronto contract security industry, finding strong support for
the NVM's main predictions. Net of the standard class and status
indicators—both individual and family-of-origin—knowing people in
diverse class positions is the best predictor of familiarity with a
broader range of cultural pursuits. In this respect, according to the
NVM, the oft-noted correlation between markers of social position (e.g.,
education and occupational prestige) and cultural omnivorousness is
(partially) spurious. People in high-status positions are more
culturally omnivorous because they have a larger volume and broader
range of network contacts.

Erickson’s NVM has been expanded and developed in subsequent work. In a
follow-up study, Kane (2004) uses the NVM to examine how differences in
the structure of social capital can help explain well-established gender
differences in cultural participation. Using data from a student sample
at an elite university in the United States, Kane finds that respondents
with denser networks are less likely to participate in cultural
activities, except those (such as sports) linked to solidarity-producing
interaction rituals (Collins 2004). More importantly, Kane finds that
more socio-demographically heterogeneous ego networks increase the
likelihood that individuals will consume high-status genres, providing
evidence of a link between network structure and the accumulation of
cultural capital as high-status signals. Importantly, all network
effects are most potent for women, providing a social-capital
explanation for their often-observed cultural-capital advantage over
men.

In the case of the United Kingdom, Warde & Tampubolon (2002) use data
from the British Household Panel Survey to examine the link between
social and cultural capital. Consistent with the NVM, they find that the
more associational and network-based ties people have—as indexed by
associational memberships and friendships—the more likely they are to
participate in a broader range of recreational and leisure activities.
Widdop (2014), for his part, builds on the distinction between “bonding”
and “bridging” social capital (Putnam, 2001) to examine how social
networks predict distinct patterns of musical consumption. Using data
from the third wave of the Taking Part Survey, conducted in a random
sample of participants in England, Widdop uses latent class analysis on
a set of items measuring participation in live musical events featuring
six genres of music (e.g., Opera, Classical, Rock & Pop, Folk, Jazz,
R&B) to divide respondents into three groups: Omnivores, Univores, and
Abstainers. Widdop measures social capital using generalized trust items
(bonding), while indexing network ties (bridging capital) using the
standard position generator differentiated across three types of role
relations: Kin, Friends, and Acquaintances.[2] Widdop finds that,
consistent with Erickson’s network variety model, omnivores have a
greater range of connections to people in different positions. However,
weaker and non-kin ties to those positions (acquaintances and friends)
help predict being in the omnivore class, whereas the array of kin ties
does not.

In a recent series of studies published in English, Cebula (2015, 2019,
2023, 2024) uses data from a sample of respondents in the Polish city of
Wrocław to examine further empirical implications of the NVM. In the
first study, based on face-to-face survey data collected in 2011, Cebula
(2015) used a two-pronged approach to measure network ties: A factor
analysis of four items aimed at measuring resources embedded in personal
networks (via resource generator items) and the self-reported frequency
of interaction with non-kin contacts outside the home.[3] The primary
outcome variable was a cultural participation scale based on
self-reported frequency of engagement in a series of cultural activities
(e.g., art museums, galleries, theater, music performances). Consistent
with the NVM, Cebula found that the more contacts elicited via the
resource generator and the more frequent interactions with non-kin
friends and acquaintances outside the home, the wider the range of
activities respondents reported consuming at high frequency.

Extending the analysis to musical taste, Cebula (2019) uses data from
the same city collected in 2016 to measure network ties in two ways. One
is based on the familiar position generator, but split into strong
(friend and family) and weak (acquaintances) ties, for fourteen
occupations distributed across the status ladder. The other is based on
questions about how many contacts a person knows who differ from them on
a series of characteristics (e.g., age, cultural pursuits, political
views, organizational affiliations); this is a measure of “heterophily”
in social connections, the obverse of the popular construct of homophily
(McPherson et al., 2001). Cebula also measured the number of
organizations to which the respondent reported belonging. The primary
outcome was a measure of “omnivorousness by composition,” constructed by
counting the number of pairs of genres classified into two distinct
categories (highbrow and popular) that the respondent reports liking.
Cebula’s results are once again consistent with the NVM: Respondents
with more acquaintances (but not stronger ties, such as friends or
relatives) across various social positions have broader musical tastes,
as do respondents with more heterogeneous personal networks (e.g.,
composed of people different from themselves). Meanwhile, the frequency
of interaction with kin ties outside the home was negatively associated
with musical taste variety, whereas associational social capital had no
statistically significant effect. Overall, Cebula’s work establishes an
empirical link between heterogeneity in social network ties and the
capacity to cross symbolic boundaries associated with cultural taste.

In a more recent paper, using data from more than a thousand residents
of Wroclaw collected in 2017, Cebula (2023) connects Erickson’s NVM with
Schultz and Breiger’s (2010) distinction between “strong” and “weak”
culture—proposing that weak tie network diversity should be more
predictive of the number of “weak” cultural pursuits while strong-tie
network diversity should predict “strong” cultural pursuits. In this
study, strong cultural pursuits are those undertaken frequently (at
least once a month), and weak cultural pursuits are those undertaken
less regularly (e.g., a few times a year). As in other studies, Cebula
constructs two indicators of network diversity: one based on the
position generator (with reported contacts split by role relations) and
the other on a scale of contacts who are different from the respondent.
The basic idea is that various types of network variety (weak and
strong) should be systematically linked to corresponding types of
cultural variety (weak and strong, respectively). Consistent with
expectations, Cebula finds that weak tie network diversity predicts the
number of weak cultural engagements but not the number of “strong”
cultural engagements. Strong-tie network diversity, on the other hand,
predicts both strong and weak cultural engagement. The volume of
heterophilous ties, on the other hand, predicts weak cultural
engagements but is not correlated with strong cultural pursuits.

Following along these lines, other recent work examines how different
forms of network connectivity help predict distinct forms of cultural
taste, a critical empirical implication of the NVM. Rather than
conceptualizing cultural and social capital as unidimensional
constructs, this work seeks to differentiate subtypes of cultural and
social capital and to investigate their linkages. For instance,
Childress and collaborators (2021) disaggregate cultural capital into
high-status forms of taste that combine inclusiveness at the level of
genres with discernment and exclusiveness at the level of specific
cultural objects nested within genres (e.g., artists or songs in the
case of music). Childress et al. hypothesize that consistent with
Erickson’s diversity principle, people whose personal network profile
consists of weak ties to others in diverse positions will have a wider
variety of tastes at the genre level, while also proposing a personal
network basis for exclusionary taste at the object level with people
whose personal network profile consists of strong ties to others in
high-status positions are likelier to display an exclusivist cultural
capital profile, where exclusivity is conceptualized as having a taste
profile biased towards objects (e.g., artist or performers) that have
received the most institutional consecration by the designated cultural
authorities (critics and established awards).

Using data from a 2018 Qualtrics panel of American respondents and the
position generator strategy to elicit weak and strong tie contacts in
the personal network, Childress et al. find that, indeed, the more weak
ties (as indicated by the acquaintance role relation) one has to people
in different occupations, the more inclusive tastes (as given by the
volume of likes) are at the genre level across three cultural domains
(movies, music, and television). However, the stronger ties (as
indicated by typing the tie as either friend or family) one has to
people in high-status occupations, the more restricted the range of
objects liked within each genre. This means that people with the most
social capital (e.g., a larger number of weak ties across positions,
combined with strong ties to people in high-status positions) display a
taste profile that combines breadth across genres with exclusivity
within them.

Summary and Empirical Expectations

In sum, recent work on the links between personal networks and culture
provides broad support for Erickson’s NVM and the associated thesis that
network variety (e.g., range and heterogeneity) is connected to cultural
variety in both active cultural participation and avowed tastes (at the
level of genres). This work also expands the scope of Erickson’s
original model to examine variation in connectivity and range across
distinct types of network ties, and their relation to different forms of
cultural participation and taste. Yet, the literature suffers from three
limitations and gaps. First, with a few exceptions, most studies
naturally focus on participation in traditional arts and on taste for
products emanating from traditional cultural industries (e.g., music,
film, television, and the arts). Secondly, position and resource
generators, along with broad-based indices of connection to dissimilar
alters, have served as the primary means of measuring volume, range, and
heterogeneity at the personal network level. Third, this focus on volume
and range, and reliance on standard position and resource generators to
measure it, may overlook or mute other forms of network composition,
such as group-based networks, which may have independent effects on
cultural tastes and practices.

Turning to the first of these observations, in relation to which
questions are asked and what “counts” as cultural participation in
survey research, we know from recent work that when we limit ourselves
to traditional forms of participation in the art and culture industry, a
substantial proportion of the population emerges as “inactive.” This
does not mean, however, that these people do nothing; instead, they
engage in forms of leisure and cultural activities that are less likely
to be captured by traditional arts- and media-based indicators. Instead,
these “invisible” leisure and culture consumption activities tend to be
centered at home (a situation more likely after the COVID pandemic) or
are only tangentially related to cultural consumption as traditionally
defined, being centered around pursuits less connected to aesthetic
engagement and more strongly connected to activities done while alone,
such as DIY practical pastimes (e.g., gardening), self-development and
cultivation of the mind (e.g., listening to audiobooks or informational
podcasts), or challenging the body via various Foucaldian technologies
of the self (e.g., fitness) (Jarness 2015; Stillerman 2023). There is no
ex ante reasons why these forms of leisure consumption should not be
subject to the network effects described in the NVM. Accordingly,
whether characteristics of the personal network relate to these more
practical or mundane forms of leisure activity in the same way they do
to traditional forms of arts and mediated consumption remains an open
question. In what follows, we use a measurement strategy designed to
capture both the conventional forms of arts and media-related
consumption and other non-standard leisure pursuits.

Secondly, the way characteristics of the personal network are measured
and defined can also be expanded. As we have seen, the main workhorse of
previous work has been the position generator (and, secondarily, the
resource generator). The beauty of the position generator is that it
provides an efficient, synoptic window into how well-connected
individuals are within the social structure. However, in defining the
idea of social “position” almost exclusively in terms of occupation and
occupational status (e.g., prestige or SEI indices), the position
generator essentially reduces social structure (in Blau’s sense) to a
single “parameter” or dimension of association, when previous work
suggests that the multidimensionality of cultural niches is particularly
relevant (Mark 2003). One approach we saw in Cebula’s work is to
supplement measures of volume and connectivity extracted from position
generators with a set of items designed to measure connectivity across
positions defined in non-occupational terms (e.g., gender, age, and so
forth). In what follows, we use a novel strategy that combines the
eliciting logic of the position generator (e.g., “how many people do you
know who are…”) but which defines position in a broader sense beyond
occupation to include such dimensions of association as race, sexuality,
religion, political ideology, nationality, gender, and urban/rural
status, while also capturing variation in the strength of the tie
between ego and the set of people mentioned in each position.

Third, adapting the position generator from an occupation-based to a
group-based measure enables a broader conceptualization of the
relationship between personal networks and cultural practices. This
shift potentially extends well-established research in the NVM tradition
by incorporating composition-oriented, group-based measures that move
beyond social class and occupational status. For example, as we already
know, personal networks are homophilously structured along non-class
demographic dimensions such as age, gender, and race, and cultural
practices and tastes are likewise segmented along these lines (McPherson
et al. 2001). Yet existing measures have made it difficult to link these
two observations, isolate the independent effects of group-based network
composition on cultural practices and tastes, or assess whether such
effects are substantively meaningful. One particularly salient
contemporary case may concern political ideology. Cultural practices and
tastes have become increasingly intertwined with political ideology
(DellaPosta 2020; Shi, Kiley, and Lynn 2025), while social ties in the
United States are also increasingly sorted along ideological lines
(Iyengar, Sood, and Lelkes 2012; Mason 2018). What remains unclear,
however, is whether ideological sorting within personal networks
directly contributes to the ideological stratification of cultural
practices themselves. In this paper, in addition to our first two
contributions, we directly address this third question.

Data and Methods

Data were collected in the second two weeks of April 2025 via Prolific,
an international, high-quality data firm (Albert and Smilek, 2023;
Douglas, Ewell & Brauer, 2023; Peer, Rothschild, Gordon, Evernden, and
Damer, 2021; Stagnaro et al., 2024). Respondents were selected under the
“representative sample” option, which quotas English-speaking US
respondents by age, gender identity, race, and political affiliation,
and compensated at Prolific’s recommended “good” rate. Respondents who
declined a commitment check or failed both attention checks were
excluded from the survey, and their data were not recorded (Berinsky et
al., 2014; Geisen, 2022). Starting from 1,258 completed surveys,
duplicates and “speeders”—defined as spending less than 1/3rd of the
median respondent time to complete the study (Zhang & Conrad, 2014)—were
dropped before analyses, reducing the analytic sample size to N = 1,243.
The data were collected as part of a larger project on cultural taste
and arts participation.

Main Outcomes

Respondents were asked to report their frequency of activity for 20
items presented in random order:

  (1) Go to a museum; (2) Go to an art gallery; (3) Go to the symphony,
  orchestra, or opera; (4) Gardening or planting; (5) Go to a carnival,
  county fair, or amusement park; (6) Go to a music concert or festival;
  (7) Go to a play, musical, or performance in a theater; (8) Go to the
  library; (9) Go to a fancy restaurant; (10) Eat fast food; (11) Go for
  a walk; (12) Go to the gym, to exercise, or do yoga; (13) Go to the
  ballet or a dance performance; (14) Go to see a movie in the theater;
  (15) Reading a novel, poem, or play; (16) Attend a sports game or
  match; (17) Do home or auto repair; (18) Go hiking, camping, or
  boating; (19) Visit a historic site or landmark; (20) Go to a
  cultural, artistic, food, or neighborhood festival.

For each item, respondents were presented with seven response
categories:

  (1) zero times/not in the past year; (2) 1 to 2 times in the past
  year; (3) 3–5 times (every few months or so); (4) 6–11 times (every
  other month or more); (5) 12–23 times (once or twice a month); (6)
  24–51 times (every other week to almost every week); (7) 52 or more
  (once a week or more).

We construct our primary outcome variables for cultural consumption and
participation from these items. To that end, we used principal component
factor analysis and retained a three-factor solution (eigenvalues > 1;
KMO = .958), which together explained 58.7% of the variance. We rotate
this solution obliquely (direct oblimin) rather than orthogonally
(varimax), since there is no substantive reason to assume that public
arts participation, everyday solitary leisure, and residual practical
leisure are uncorrelated with one another; oblimin lets the data, rather
than the rotation method, determine the association among these
dimensions. We generated cultural consumption and participation
variables for each respondent from the predicted factor scores for each
observation, standardized to have a mean of 0 and a standard deviation
of 1.

Public Arts Participation

The first factor accounted for 42.8% of the variance. As seen in Figure
1, Factor 1 is characterized by high levels of public arts
participation, including symphony and opera attendance (loading = 0.88),
dance performances (0.88), theater or musical performances (0.84), art
galleries (0.83), live music concerts (0.82), museum visits (0.80),
festivals (0.77), historic site visits (0.71), and movie theater
attendance (0.69).

Solitary Leisure Activities

The second factor accounted for 9.1% of the variance and is
characterized by recreational leisure activities including “going for
walks” (loading = 0.85), exercise or athletic activities (0.49), reading
novels (0.43), gardening (0.33), going to the library (0.33), and hiking
(0.29). We interpret this factor as everyday solitary leisure. The third
factor accounts for 6.8% of the variance, and we interpret it as
essentially a residual category, with loadings on gardening (0.54), home
auto repair (0.41), hiking or camping (0.23), and a strong negative
loading for fast food consumption (–0.69). Because we rotate obliquely
rather than orthogonally, we also note that all three activity factors
are only weakly correlated with one another (|r| ≤ .25), consistent with
treating them as substantively distinct outcomes.

[Figure 1 About Here]

Main Predictors

The main predictors in this study are constructed from a factor analysis
of a battery of items designed to capture the range and composition of
the personal networks of U.S. respondents across a wide range of
possible dimensions of association (Blau 1977) and connectivity strength
along the classic weak-to-strong tie continuum (Granovetter 1973). To
that end, respondents answered two network modules: one for weak ties
and one for strong ties. The prompt for weak ties was as follows:

  “We're now going to ask you some questions about all the people that
  you are acquainted with, meaning that you know their name and would
  stop and talk at least for a moment if you ran into the person on the
  street or in a shopping mall. Some of these questions may seem unusual
  but they are important to understand about social networks. How many
  people that you are acquainted with…”

The prompt for strong ties differed in the following ways:

  “We're now going to ask you some questions about all the people that
  you are close with and trust. For example, good friends, people you
  discuss important matters with, or trust for advice, or trust with
  money. Some of these questions may seem unusual but they are important
  to understand about social networks. How many people that you are
  close with and trust…”

For both the weak ties and strong ties modules, respondents were asked
to identify the number of personal connections across the following 18
groups:

(1) Are gay or lesbian or queer or transgender; (2) Attend religious
      services on a regular basis; (3) Attend religious services rarely
      or never; (4) Are strongly liberal; (5) Are strongly
      conservative; (6) Are Asian or Asian American; (7) Are Hispanic or
      Latino or Latinx; (8) Are Black or African American; (9) Are
      white; (10) Own a second home; (11) Were born in or are from a
      country that is not the United States; (12) Are MENA (of Middle
      Eastern or North African descent); (13) Are Native Hawaiian or
      Pacific Islander; (14) Are American Indian or Alaska Native; (15)
      Live in a large city (over 250,000); (16) Live in a rural area or
      small town (less than 50,000); (17) Are men; (18) Are women.

For each group, respondents answered on the following five-point,
ordered scale with the following options: None/0 people; 1 person; 2 to
5 people; 6 to 10 people; more than 10 people. For both weak and strong
ties, we similarly rely on an exploratory principal component factor
analysis to classify items into broader classes, again rotating the
solution obliquely (direct oblimin) rather than orthogonally (varimax):
there is no theoretical reason to expect that knowing more ideologically
liberal alters and knowing more ideologically conservative alters are
uncorrelated, since both may simply reflect a respondent’s overall
network size or sociability rather than opposite poles of a single
ideological spectrum. In both cases, we retain three-factor solutions
(eigenvalues > 1; KMOs = .938 for weak ties and .935 for strong ties),
with each solution explaining approximately 61% of the total variance.
As we did for the cultural participation and leisure activities items,
we calculated personal network variety and composition variables for
each respondent from the predicted factor scores. These scores are
standardized to have a mean of zero and a standard deviation of 1.

Network Variety

Factor 1 explains 20.1% of the variance in the weak-tie model and 25.4%
in the strong-tie model. Across both weak- and strong-tie networks, this
factor loads positively across a wide range of social groups rather than
clustering around a single category. In the weak tie model, Factor 1 is
anchored by high loadings on knowing Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander
(.85), American Indian (.80), MENA (.76), and Asian (.59) individuals,
with additional loadings on class-coded ties (second-home owners; .56)
and immigrant-origin contacts (knowing someone born outside the U.S.;
.45); the strong tie model shows a highly similar pattern, including
strong loadings on Pacific Islander (.87), MENA (.84), American Indian
(.81), Asian (.67), immigrant-origin (.62), and second-home owner (.60)
ties. We interpret Factor 1 as capturing network variety rather than
ties to any particular group or orientation, as we show in the
supplementary analysis in the appendix.

Network Composition

In both weak and strong tie networks, Factor 2, which explains 23.9% of
the variance for weak ties and 14.0% for strong ties, loads most
strongly on left-leaning ideology and aligned groups. For weak ties,
Factor 2 is anchored by knowing very liberal (.78) and LGBTQ (.76)
individuals, those with low church attendance (.62) and Hispanic/Latine
contacts (.62), with a secondary loading on urban ties (.56). The strong
tie model shows a similar concentration on very liberal (.76) and LGBTQ
(.69) ties, alongside low church attendance (.49) and urban (.45)
contacts. In turn, Factor 3, which explains 17.3% of the variance for
weak ties and 21.8% for strong ties, loads most strongly on conservative
and religious social environments. In the weak tie model, this factor is
anchored by knowing very conservative individuals (.84) and frequent
churchgoers (.70), with secondary loadings on rural ties (.68) and
second-home owners (.38); the strong tie model is centered on similarly
strong loadings for knowing white (.80), very conservative (.79), women
(.70), and frequent churchgoing (.70) contacts, alongside rural ties
(.69), indicating that for strong ties this factor also picks up a
broader conventional/mainstream social profile alongside political
conservatism.

We interpret Factor 3 as capturing right-leaning ideology and aligned
groups, which remains conceptually distinct from the variety-oriented
networks captured by Factor 1 and the liberal-aligned groups of Factor
2, though under the oblique rotation we use here these three dimensions
are allowed to (and do) correlate rather than being forced to
independence: variety correlates modestly with both liberal (r = .35
weak, .26 strong) and conservative (r = .25 weak, .44 strong)
composition, and liberal and conservative composition are themselves
modestly positively correlated with one another (r = .39 weak, .28
strong) rather than negatively related, indicating that knowing more
ideologically liberal and more ideologically conservative alters are not
opposite poles of a single spectrum but partly co-occur, plausibly
reflecting respondents’ overall network breadth. We thus refer to Factor
1 as weak and strong-tie variety, and to Factors 2 and 3 as weak and
strong-tie liberal and conservative composition.

[Figure 2 About Here]

Other Predictors

Mutivariable models adjust for a series of possible confounders (e.g.,
variables that could be correlated with both cultural consumption and
the range and composition of personal networks) including gender
identification (woman; man; non-binary/trans/other), highest educational
degree completed (HS or less, some college, college degree, graduate
degree) childhood arts exposure (never; very rarely; somewhat rarely;
sometimes; somewhat frequently; very frequently; all the time), age,
ethnoracial identity (White, Black, Hispanic/Latine, Asian
American/Pacific Islander, mixed/other), household income (13-point
scale), and political ideology, which is constructed on a seven point,
liberal-to-conservative scale averaged from two separate self-reports of
ideological placement on economic and social issues, respectively.
Descriptive statistics and the correlation matrix are provided in the
appendix.

Results

Table 1 presents OLS regression models predicting arts participation as
a function of weak- and strong-tie network variety in Models 1 and 2,
with measures of ideological network composition added in Models 3 and
4; diagnostic tests indicated no problematic multicollinearity among the
included predictors.

Across all models, and consistent with the network variety model, both
weak- and strong-tie variety predict increasing frequencies of public
arts participation. The coefficient estimate for the strong-tie network
variable is more than twice that for the weak-tie variable—a
statistically significant difference (F(1, 1213) = 19.41, p <
.001)—indicating that a diverse range of strong ties has a greater
effect on driving public arts participation. This difference is
illustrated in Figure 3, which plots the predicted score in the public
arts participation factor on the y-axis as a function of the
respondent’s score in the strong-tie (solid line) and weak-tie (dashed
line) variety factors on the x-axis. The Figure shows that a one-unit
increase in the strong tie variety score corresponds to roughly a
half-standard deviation increase in arts participation, after adjusting
for other socio-demographic factors. Note also that the effect of
weak-tie variety is more strongly mediated by the inclusion of the
socio-demographic factors in Model 2, and is reduced by about half
compared to Model 1. The effect of strong tie variety on public arts
participation, on the other hand, is almost entirely direct, with the
estimate being only slightly lower in Model 2 than in Model 1.

The statistically significant sociodemographic effects in Model 2 are
consistent with what we would expect from previous work. Education and
childhood exposure to the arts increase the contemporaneous frequency of
public arts consumption. In contrast, participation in the public arts
declines with age and is higher among self-identified white respondents
than among AAPI (p < .001) or multiracial respondents (p = .005); the
corresponding contrast with Hispanic/Latine respondents is in the same
direction but only marginally significant (p = .07). Interestingly, we
find that political ideology has a substantively small but statistically
significant net effect: more conservative respondents report a higher
frequency of participation in public arts than liberals. This contrasts
with previous work that has examined the impact of political ideology on
self-reported taste for cultural items, which generally finds that
liberals like a broader range of cultural items (Rawlings and Childress
2023), suggesting a disjuncture between the effects of political
ideology on self-reported taste and participation.

[Figure 3 About Here]

As shown in Models 3 and 4, adding ideological network composition does
little to attenuate the effects of network variety for either weak or
strong ties, suggesting that the factor analyses capture distinct
sources of variance in the personal networks of U.S. respondents. After
adjusting for relevant sociodemographic covariates in Model 4, we find
that weak ties to people in liberal positions are associated with lower
levels of arts participation (b = -.13, p = .001); this is the only one
of the four composition coefficients that reaches conventional
significance in this model, as strong-tie liberal composition (b = -.04,
p = .27), weak-tie conservative composition (b = .01, p = .73), and
strong-tie conservative composition (b = .03, p = .40) are not
statistically distinguishable from zero. Note that the direct positive
effect of conservative political ideology on arts participation in Model
2 (b = .03, p = .03) is nonetheless fully mediated by personal network
composition: when ideological network composition is included in Model
4, the coefficient estimate is now close to zero and no longer
statistically significant (b = -.01, p = .46), suggesting that the
greater likelihood of those who identify as conservative reporting
higher levels of arts participation is explained by their broader
pattern of network composition rather than any single ideological tie
category, consistent with a homophily effect (Mark 1998; McPherson et
al. 2001).

[Table 1 About Here]

Table 2 examines the network predictors of everyday solitary leisure,
again focusing on weak- and strong-tie network variety in Models 1 and
2, with measures of ideological network composition added in Models 3
and 4. In contrast to public-arts models, the variety of weak- and
strong-tie personal networks exerts countervailing influences. Across
all specifications, weak-tie variety is positively associated with
everyday solitary leisure, whereas strong-tie variety is negatively
associated, net of other predictors. Substantively, a one-unit increase
in the predicted factor score for weak-tie variety corresponds to an
increase of approximately 0.13 to 0.21 standard deviations in solitary
leisure across the four model specifications. In contrast, greater
strong-tie variety is associated with a roughly 0.08 to 0.17 standard
deviation decrease in the frequency of engagement in everyday leisure
activities. As before, we observe a somewhat stronger mediation of the
weak-tie variety effect by socio-demographic variables than for the
strong-tie variety, although not to the same extent as in the public
arts participation models. Overall, it seems that, given the strong
positive effect of variety in strong ties on more active forms of arts
participation, they function here as a mechanism to funnel people into
those more public pursuits, thereby depressing participation in
competing solitary leisure activities. Weak ties, in contrast, given
their less demanding nature, facilitate involvement across the entire
range of leisure and cultural consumption activities.

This countervailing pattern is illustrated in Figure 4, which plots the
predicted score in the solitary leisure factor on the y-axis as a
function of the respondent’s score in the strong-tie (solid line) and
weak-tie (dashed line) variety factors on the x-axis, following the same
predicted-margins specification used for Figure 3. The two predicted
lines cross near the sample mean of the variety factors, with weak-tie
variety associated with higher predicted solitary leisure and strong-tie
variety associated with lower predicted solitary leisure across the
observed range of network variety, after adjusting for other
socio-demographic factors.

[Figure 4 About Here]

Looking at Model 2, we see that the effects of other socio-demographic
variables are similar to those observed in the public arts participation
models, though there are also notable contrasts. Education increases the
frequency of engagement in more solitary leisure activities, as does
exposure to childhood arts, whose effect attenuates somewhat but remains
statistically significant once network composition variables are
introduced in Model 4 (b = .04, p = .02). Age does not affect solitary
leisure, which makes sense given the less demanding nature of these
activities compared to participation in the public arts. Higher
household income increases solitary leisure activities (in contrast to
its null effect on public arts participation), as does
self-identification as a woman, consistent with previously observed
gendering of such activities, such as gardening, yoga, and,
particularly, fiction reading (Long 2003). Finally, we also observe a
net effect of political ideology on solitary leisure activities, with
liberals more likely to engage in them than conservatives.

As before, adding ideological network composition does little to
attenuate the effects of network variety. In Models 3 and 4, strong ties
to persons in “liberal” positions are positively associated with
everyday solitary leisure (b = .11, p = .02), and weak-tie liberal
composition shows a positive association of similar magnitude that falls
just short of conventional significance (b = .09, p = .06). Ties to
conservative positions show, at most, a comparably weak positive
association for strong ties (b = .09, p = .09) and none for weak ties (b
= .02, p = .62), so we read this pattern cautiously as suggesting that
liberal-leaning ties are the more consistent compositional correlate of
solitary leisure, rather than as evidence of a sharp
liberal/conservative asymmetry. Furthermore, as observed for public arts
participation, the association between political ideological
self-placement and solitary leisure in Model 2 (b = -.04, p = .01) is
fully mediated by network composition: the Model 4 estimate falls to
near zero and loses significance (b = -.01, p = .66), suggesting that
the higher likelihood of liberals reporting engagement in everyday
leisure is explained by their broader pattern of network composition
rather than any single ideological tie category, also consistent with a
homophily effect (Mark 1998; McPherson et al. 2001).

[Table 2 About Here]

As a discriminant-validity check on our network composition measures, we
re-estimate this same four-model sequence using the third, residual
factor from our activities battery (Table A3). This factor loads on
gardening, home or auto repair, and hiking or camping, and negatively on
fast food consumption, and we interpret it as capturing everyday
DIY-practical leisure rather than engagement with the arts or with
solitary cultural consumption. If ideological network composition
captures something specific about cultural and leisure participation,
rather than a generic tendency toward leisure engagement of any kind,
its effects should not extend to this residual domain.

Consistent with this expectation, none of the four composition
coefficients approaches statistical significance in Models 3 or 4 of
Table A3, and formal Wald tests confirm that the composition block adds
no explanatory power over models with variety alone (χ²(4) = 4.05, p =
.399) or over models that already include the full set of
socio-demographic controls (χ²(4) = 7.07, p = .132). This null pattern,
set alongside the associations we observe for public arts participation
and solitary leisure, supports treating our composition measures as
tapping domain-specific cultural and leisure engagement rather than an
artifact correlated with any activity measure in the battery.

[Table A3 About Here]

Discussion and Concluding Remarks

Research on the relationship between networks and cultural taste has
relied heavily, and productively, on the NVM, finding across a range of
empirical sites and contexts that variety in networks and cultural
tastes and activities are linked. In this paper, we identify three
potentially productive supplements to this line of research and put them
to empirical work. Broadly, we find that for the standard suite of
cultural activities and practices most commonly measured, the basic
findings of the NVM are robust to a novel conceptualization of how to
measure network variety. Yet by broadening the scope of what “counts” as
cultural participation, we find that for more everyday, solitary leisure
activities, network variety in weak and strong ties operates in opposing
directions, with those with more variety in their weak ties still
engaging in more of these cultural practices as the NVM might suggest,
while those with more strong-tie variety engaging in them less. Taken
together, these findings suggest that network variety may not operate as
a uniform engine of cultural omnivorousness. We also find that network
composition is structured mainly around political ideology and
ideologically-aligned groups, with those with liberal-leaning weak ties
engaging in less conventional arts participation, which those with more
liberal strong ties, and to a lesser extent liberal weak ties, seem to
be making up for with more everyday solitary leisure. We further show
that these composition effects are domain-specific rather than a generic
correlate of any activity: an identical model predicting a residual,
practical leisure factor (e.g., gardening or home repair) unrelated to
arts or cultural consumption shows no association with network
composition, supporting our interpretation of ideological sorting as a
mechanism specific to cultural and leisure engagement rather than an
artifact of general sociability. In what follows, we discuss these
potential contributions in more detail, our limitations, and ideas for
future research.
With respect to cultural participation, expanding the analytic scope
beyond conventional attendance-based measures reveals distinct
configurations that have previously been obscured in the literature.
That individuals with greater strong-tie variety engage in fewer
solitary leisure activities is perhaps unsurprising, yet this pattern
challenges an implicit assumption in the literature that greater network
variety uniformly corresponds to greater cultural participation; a “more
is more” assumption implicit in the NVM. More broadly, we believe
attendance-based measures of cultural participation have (at least in
part) achieved prominence not because of their theoretical centrality,
but because of their close alignment with state cultural policy and
public funding infrastructures. Our findings suggest that some
individuals otherwise classified as culturally “inactive” may instead be
differently active in domains that standard attendance-based measures
fail to capture. While these cultural practices may be of less interest
to tourism boards, asking about them reveals interesting patterns of
network associations both within and beyond the scope of the NVM. The
problem is further compounded by a heavy reliance on participation in
highbrow fine arts, forms that have experienced long-term decline due to
limited cohort replacement (Peterson and Rossman 2012), thereby possibly
inflating the number of misclassified “inactives.” This observation
echoes Bourdieu’s (1993) observation that defining the boundaries of
legitimate cultural activity is a fundamentally political, rather than
purely intellectual, act. While boundaries around what counts as
cultural participation undoubtedly exist, they remain under-theorized
and insufficiently specified. We view our contribution on this front as
necessarily modest, but suggest that future research must engage this
issue more deliberately and systematically.
Likewise, an overreliance on position- and resource-based generators has
facilitated comparisons across studies but may also have narrowed the
conceptualization of network variety. Incorporating position generators
that use sociodemographic group–based measures may offer several
advantages. First, group-based position generators better align with how
variation is theorized across many sociological subfields, where
diversity is typically defined in terms of sociodemographic groups
rather than occupational positions (Blau 1977; McPherson et al. 2001;
Mark 2003). In this respect, the continued reliance on occupations to
measure network variety is increasingly out of step with how variety and
diversity are more broadly conceptualized in sociology, which (perhaps
unfortunately) privileges identity-based distinctions while sidelining
class and economic heterogeneity (Childress and Lizardo 2026). Second,
sociodemographic group–based measures provide greater theoretical
leverage for understanding cultural participation and taste. For
example, networks composed primarily of particular occupations (e.g.,
lawyers or carpenters) are comparatively limited in what they reveal
about social segmentation in cultural practices. In contrast, networks
structured more explicitly along class, racial, gendered, or ideological
lines may more directly map onto the symbolic boundaries that organize
cultural engagement. Again, this is not to suggest that we have
identified the correct group-based measures, nor that occupation-based
and group-based position generators should be treated as equivalent in a
pro forma sense. Instead, we argue that further investigation along
these lines is both warranted and necessary.
Finally, our findings contribute to the growing literature on cultural
tastes and the ideological segmentation of everyday life by
demonstrating that ideological sorting within personal networks affects
cultural participation and leisure practices. To our knowledge, this is
the first study to show that ideological network composition plays a
central role in structuring cultural engagement. Whereas prior research
has treated political ideology primarily as an individual attribute, our
results indicate that the relationship between ideology and cultural
participation operates mainly through patterned social environments.
Across both cultural domains we examine, the direct association between
respondents’ ideological self-placement and participation is fully
mediated by personal network composition, suggesting that cultural
stratification is organized relationally rather than dispositionally
(Crossley 2015; Emirbayer 1997). In this respect, our findings parallel
a core insight of the network variety model: just as the correlation
between markers of social position and cultural omnivorousness is partly
spurious when network variety is unobserved, recently documented
associations between political ideology and cultural tastes may likewise
be overstated when ideological sorting in personal networks is not taken
into account (DellaPosta et al. 2015). This raises the possibility that
patterns often attributed to core psychological differences between
liberals and conservatives (e.g., Jost, 2021) are, at least in part,
rooted in social structure.
Our finding that weak ties to liberals are associated with lower levels
of conventional arts participation likely reflects that our arts
participation factor loads most heavily on conventionally highbrow
activities (e.g., ballet or dance performances, theater, and symphony or
opera). As prior work shows, liberals tend to express broader tastes
across cultural objects and to invest in variety as a marker of cultural
capital (Rawlings and Childress 2023; Rogers and Jost 2022), whereas
conventional highbrow cultural forms have increasingly come to be
appreciated (and defended) as legitimate culture by conservatives
(Purhonen and Heikkilä 2016). More broadly, these findings suggest that
network-based ideological sorting provides a promising bridge between
research on cultural taste and emerging frameworks on affective
polarization, in which cultural participation practices function as
sites through which ideological social boundaries are enacted and
reproduced.
Taken together, we believe the NVM remains a highly relevant and robust
summation of the relationship between social networks and cultural
taste. We see our work as adding to the NVM tradition by expanding its
scope into unexplored terrain: by simultaneously accounting for both
variety and composition in networks when studying cultural practices and
tastes, and by broadening the range of cultural activities and practices
under consideration. We also note that the relationship between networks
and taste may be structured by previously unconsidered factors, such as
the ideological composition of networks. We believe this may be
particularly worthy of further investigation.

APPENDIX

[]Figure A1. Correlation Heat Map of Continuous and Ordinal Predictor
Variables.

Table A1. Descriptive Statistics of the Variables Used in the Analysis.

[]

Network Variety

To further assess the interpretation of Factor 1 as capturing network
variety, we examined its association with independently constructed
variety count measures of the number of distinct social groups
respondents reported knowing. Variety counts were calculated as the
number of groups for which respondents reported knowing at least one
person, and in Table A2, associations are reported as Pearson
correlations. For strong ties, the network variety factor remains the
most strongly correlated of the three factors with these observed counts
(r = .79, versus .54 and .73 for liberal and conservative composition,
respectively). For weak ties, this discriminant pattern is less clean
under the oblique rotation: the liberal-composition factor correlates
about as strongly with the raw group count (r = .76) as does the variety
factor itself (r = .70), and conservative composition is not far behind
(r = .62). This is an expected consequence of allowing the three
weak-tie factors to correlate rather than forcing them to independence:
respondents with broader weak-tie networks tend to know more people
across all eighteen groups, including ideologically-coded ones, so the
ideological composition factors partly track sheer network breadth as
well as ideological content. Results are substantively similar when
using a stricter threshold that requires respondents to report knowing
two or more people in a given group. We therefore read Factor 1 as
capturing cross-group breadth most cleanly for strong ties, while for
weak ties this validation check is suggestive rather than conclusive,
and we interpret the weak-tie composition estimates in Tables 1–2 and A3
accordingly.

Table A2. Correlation Matrix of Factor Scores for Strong and Weak Tie
Network Variety and Composition with the Count of Positions Respondents
are Connected to.

Network Variety and Composition on the Residual Factor.

[]

[1] Coauthorship is equal.

[2] The position generator (see Lin et al., 2001) is a network,
amembershipnd social capital survey interview elicitation technique in
which respondents are presented with a list of social positions
(typically occupational titles, such as doctors, lawyers, plumbers,
nurses, carpenters) and are then asked whether they know someone in that
position as well as other characteristics of the contact (e.g., gender,
race, type of tie).

[3] The resource generator (see Van Der Gaag & Snijders, 2 005) is a
variation of the position generator strategy in which respondents are
asked whether they have contacts who can help with various requests,
problems, or services. This approach taps the extent to which resources
are embedded in a person’s network, allowing access in times of need.
